transcript:
Fireflies.ai Transcript

Meeting: Helios Health — security + approvals for case study (public vs private claims)
Date: 2025-10-07
Time: 10:00 AM PT
Duration: 41 min
Recorded by: Fireflies.ai

Attendees
- Avery Johnson (Redwood Inference) — Enterprise AE
- Michael Grant (Redwood Inference) — Legal
- Markus Klein (Redwood Inference) — Solutions Engineering
- Megan O'Connor (Helios Health) — Legal Counsel
- Dr. Lila Patel (Helios Health) — Director, Compliance
- Jason Wu (Helios Health) — Security Architect

Summary (auto-generated)
Helios Health reviewed what Redwood can state publicly in a case study, focusing on HIPAA/PHI risk, security posture claims, and approval workflow. Helios prefers anonymization for the first publication and requires metrics to be expressed as ranges with clear measurement caveats. Redwood agreed to provide a redline-friendly consent form, a claim menu, and an anonymized story outline.

Topics (auto-generated)
1) What counts as “public” statements + brand/marketing constraints
2) Attribution options (logo/name vs anonymized)
3) Metrics: ranges, baselines, and measurement methodology
4) Security/compliance claims: audit logs, KMS, data retention, SOC 2
5) Approval workflow + review windows + revocation

Questions (auto-generated)
- Can Redwood mention Helios by name or only as an anonymized healthcare org?
- What metrics can be disclosed publicly, if any?
- Can Redwood mention “HIPAA” or “BAA” in the write-up?
- What is Helios’ internal approval chain and timing expectations?

Action items (auto-generated)
- Redwood to send revised consent form + claim menu
- Helios to confirm attribution preference and acceptable phrasing
- Redwood to propose metric ranges and footnotes

Transcript

00:00 Avery Johnson: Cool, alright. Thanks everyone for making time. This is Avery from Redwood. Goal today is pretty narrow: for the Helios story, what are the compliance constraints, what can we say publicly, and what does your approval process look like so we don’t trip any wires.

00:14 Avery Johnson: I’ve got Michael here from our legal team and Markus from solutions engineering. Do you all want to do quick intros?

00:21 Megan O'Connor: Sure. Megan O’Connor, legal counsel. I cover vendor contracting and marketing approvals, unfortunately. [laughs]

00:29 Dr. Lila Patel: Lila Patel, compliance. Mostly privacy program and security reviews for third parties.

00:35 Jason Wu: Jason Wu, security architect. I’m on the team that’s been evaluating the VPC deployment.

00:42 Avery Johnson: Awesome. And just to level set, we’re not trying to force you into anything public. The program has options: reference calls only, quotes only, anonymized case study, or logo + named story. We’ll follow whatever is comfortable.

00:57 Markus Klein: And on the technical side, we can keep diagrams high level. Like boxes and arrows without subnets and account IDs.

01:04 Dr. Lila Patel: Yes, please. [laughs] That’s exactly the sort of thing we can’t have in the wild.

01:09 Avery Johnson: Great. So maybe starting question: are you open to being named publicly at all? Like “Helios Health uses Redwood Private” kind of statement.

01:20 Megan O'Connor: At this time, no. Our preference is anonymized. I can’t say “never,” but for a first one, we’d want it to be “US-based healthcare provider” or similar.

01:31 Avery Johnson: Got it. So no logo, no company name.

01:34 Megan O'Connor: Correct. Also no employee names. No photos. If there are quotes, they need to be attributed to a title only, and even then we’d like to review the title specificity.

01:46 Michael Grant: That’s workable. We can use “Director of ML Platform” or “Security Architect” without names, or even “Helios team” if needed.

01:55 Dr. Lila Patel: Titles are okay, but again, keep it generic. We have a fairly small team and it can become identifiable.

02:03 Markus Klein: Understood. So like “Compliance lead” rather than “Director of Compliance.”

02:07 Dr. Lila Patel: Exactly.

02:10 Avery Johnson: Okay. Second question: content-wise, we’d want to highlight why you chose private deployment, what constraints you had, and what outcomes. Anything off-limits there?

02:24 Dr. Lila Patel: Anything that implies patient data went to an external party is sensitive. You can’t say “we send PHI to Redwood” obviously.

02:33 Avery Johnson: We definitely won’t.

02:35 Dr. Lila Patel: Even if it’s not true, it can be interpreted that way. So language like “patient notes” or “clinical records” should not appear.

02:44 Markus Klein: We can phrase the use case as “regulated text workflows” or “sensitive documents.”

02:50 Jason Wu: Yeah, and avoid saying the model sees raw data. In our design it’s isolated in VPC, but still, we don’t want to litigate that in marketing.

03:00 Avery Johnson: Makes sense. So focus on deployment pattern and controls, not specific data types.

03:06 Megan O'Connor: Exactly.

03:09 Michael Grant: Also on HIPAA: do you want us to mention HIPAA at all?

03:14 Dr. Lila Patel: Not in a public case study. We can say “regulated environment” or “healthcare compliance requirements.” But “HIPAA-compliant” is a claim we avoid in marketing unless it’s very tightly controlled.

03:27 Michael Grant: Understood. We’ll avoid “HIPAA compliant” and “BAA” references publicly.

03:33 Jason Wu: You can say “supports customer compliance programs” type language. Just not “certified for” or “compliant with.”

03:41 Avery Johnson: Great call-out.

03:43 Avery Johnson: What about security control mentions. We usually say things like: VPC deployment, customer-managed KMS keys, audit logs, RBAC, SSO. Are those okay?

03:56 Dr. Lila Patel: Those are generally okay if they’re factual and not presented as a certification. But I want to be careful: “customer-managed keys” is okay, “HSM” might not be, depending.

04:09 Jason Wu: KMS mention is fine. Don’t mention our cloud provider. And don’t mention regions.

04:16 Markus Klein: So we should avoid “AWS KMS” specifically, just “KMS integration.”

04:20 Jason Wu: Yes.

04:22 Megan O'Connor: And with audit logs, you can state there are audit logs and what kind of events they include at a high level. But not “we retain logs for X days” unless it’s generic.

04:35 Avery Johnson: We can say “configurable retention” and “exportable.”

04:39 Jason Wu: Export format mention—like JSON—is fine. But not references to our SIEM by name.

04:47 Markus Klein: Okay. “Forwardable to a customer SIEM.”

04:52 Dr. Lila Patel: That works.

04:55 Avery Johnson: Now, metrics. We know this is the tricky part. We’d like to include outcomes like latency improvement or cost per token reduction or reliability. What’s allowed?

05:08 Megan O'Connor: We do not publish exact numbers for vendor performance. If you want to include anything, it needs to be ranges and it cannot be tied to volumes.

05:18 Avery Johnson: Ranges like “reduced p95 latency by 30–50%” kind of thing?

05:23 Megan O'Connor: That’s closer. Also we’d want a footnote that it’s based on internal measurements and results may vary, and that it’s dependent on configuration.

05:34 Markus Klein: We can do that. Also we can avoid “p95” maybe and say “tail latency” generally.

05:39 Jason Wu: “p95” is fine, but don’t include absolute milliseconds.

05:44 Dr. Lila Patel: And don’t include baseline systems or previous vendors by name.

05:50 Avery Johnson: Understood.

05:52 Avery Johnson: What about reliability. Like “improved uptime” or “reduced incident rate.”

05:58 Megan O'Connor: You can say “improved availability” but not “99.99” or similar.

06:04 Michael Grant: So no explicit SLA numbers.

06:06 Megan O'Connor: Right.

06:09 Jason Wu: You can talk about “fallback routing” conceptually, but don’t say what we fall back to.

06:15 Markus Klein: Like “policy-based routing across compatible model variants” without naming models.

06:20 Jason Wu: Exactly.

06:22 Avery Johnson: For cost: can we say “reduced unit cost per token” in a range?

06:28 Dr. Lila Patel: Maybe, but it’s still sensitive. If you do, keep it very broad, and don’t imply spending.

06:36 Megan O'Connor: I’d prefer no cost numbers at all in the first publication. If you need it, do qualitative: “meaningfully reduced,” “improved efficiency.”

06:47 Avery Johnson: That’s fair. We can do a version with only qualitative results.

06:51 Markus Klein: Or we can say “lowered infrastructure overhead” without saying dollars.

06:56 Jason Wu: Yeah.

06:58 Avery Johnson: Okay. Approval workflow. What does it look like for you? If we draft a 900-word story and a 1-page PDF, who needs to sign off and what timeline should we plan for?

07:12 Megan O'Connor: For anything public: marketing, legal, compliance, and our security leadership. Marketing is the slowest, candidly. Minimum 10 business days review. If it’s anonymized and no logo, it can be quicker, but still assume 10.

07:29 Avery Johnson: Okay, 10 business days.

07:31 Megan O'Connor: And we need final approval, not “deemed approved if no response.”

07:38 Michael Grant: Understood. Our standard consent language has a review window; we can adjust to require explicit written approval.

07:47 Dr. Lila Patel: Also, we need to ensure there’s a revocation clause. If circumstances change, we need to be able to pull it.

07:55 Michael Grant: We have revocation language, but it sometimes has constraints around already-distributed materials.

08:02 Megan O'Connor: Right, we’d want: you stop using it going forward, and you take down web pages within a reasonable time.

08:10 Michael Grant: That’s standard. We can propose “commercially reasonable efforts within 10 business days” for web properties.

08:17 Megan O'Connor: That’s acceptable.

08:19 Avery Johnson: Another question: can we still do private reference calls even if the case study is anonymized?

08:26 Megan O'Connor: Potentially. Separate approval. And calls would need prep and an agenda. Also, no recording.

08:34 Avery Johnson: Totally.

08:36 Dr. Lila Patel: And limit frequency. We’ve had bad experiences being overused.

08:41 Avery Johnson: We can put a cap, like one call per month max, and always coordinated via your CSM.

08:47 Megan O'Connor: Put it in writing.

08:49 Avery Johnson: Will do.

09:00 Markus Klein: On anonymization, when we say “US-based healthcare provider,” would you allow “mid-size” vs “large”? Or any descriptors like “multi-state”?

09:10 Dr. Lila Patel: Avoid multi-state. Avoid number of hospitals, clinics, patients, any of that. “Healthcare organization” is safest.

09:20 Jason Wu: Also avoid mentioning our EHR vendor.

09:24 Markus Klein: Yep.

09:26 Avery Johnson: And architecture diagrams: if we keep it as “Customer VPC -> Redwood Private control plane -> GPU nodes,” no mention of IP ranges, no cloud provider, no region.

09:37 Jason Wu: That’s fine. But I’d still want to review the diagram.

09:40 Avery Johnson: Yep, absolutely.

09:43 Michael Grant: One thing we get asked by prospects: certifications. Redwood has SOC 2 Type II. Are we allowed to say “Redwood is SOC 2 Type II” in the story?

09:55 Megan O'Connor: You can say it about yourselves, but do not imply it covers our environment or that it’s an endorsement.

10:03 Dr. Lila Patel: And don’t say “Helios selected Redwood because SOC2.” You can say “evaluated vendor security posture” and “SOC2 report available under NDA.”

10:14 Michael Grant: That’s helpful.

10:16 Avery Johnson: Great. Then we’ll keep the public story as: “Helios evaluated a private inference deployment; key requirements: data isolation, audit logs, key management; outcome: improved latency consistency and operational visibility.”

10:31 Dr. Lila Patel: “Operational visibility” is good.

10:34 Jason Wu: Latency consistency is okay if it’s not numeric.

10:37 Avery Johnson: Maybe “reduced tail latency variability” without numbers.

10:42 Megan O'Connor: Yes.

10:45 Markus Klein: Also the part about “automatic fallback policies” — that might read like we’re doing something without control. We should say “customer-configured fallback.”

10:53 Jason Wu: Thank you. Exactly.

10:56 Avery Johnson: Noted.

11:00 Avery Johnson: Can we mention the deployment type as “Private/VPC”? Or do you want us to just say “private deployment.”

11:08 Dr. Lila Patel: “Private deployment” is fine. “VPC” is okay but it implies a specific cloud. I know VPC is generic-ish but it’s also not.

11:17 Markus Klein: We could say “customer network boundary” or “private network deployment.”

11:22 Jason Wu: Private network deployment is fine.

11:25 Avery Johnson: Ok.

11:27 Avery Johnson: And in terms of review mechanics: is it Word doc via email? Google doc? What works.

11:34 Megan O'Connor: Send a Word doc. Track changes. No shared doc links outside our domain.

11:41 Avery Johnson: Ok.

11:43 Markus Klein: That’s fine.

11:45 Avery Johnson: Last topic: disclaimers. We usually add a metrics disclaimer and a “results vary” line. Anything else you require?

11:54 Dr. Lila Patel: Add a line that the story does not include sensitive data and that security configurations are customer-specific.

12:03 Michael Grant: We can include that.

12:05 Megan O'Connor: And no implication of endorsement. Like don’t say “Helios recommends Redwood.”

12:11 Avery Johnson: Yep.

12:13 Markus Klein: And if there are quotes, we’ll keep them about process: “deployment was straightforward,” “support was responsive,” “met our security requirements.” Not “best vendor.”

12:23 Megan O'Connor: Exactly.

12:26 Avery Johnson: Okay. I think that covers it. Before we wrap, anything else you want to flag? Any absolute no-go words besides HIPAA/BAA and PHI?

12:37 Dr. Lila Patel: “Patient.” “Clinical.” “Medical record.” Just avoid that category.

12:43 Jason Wu: And don’t mention our internal tool names.

12:46 Avery Johnson: Great.

12:48 Michael Grant: We’ll send the updated consent form. Megan, would you prefer it as a standalone marketing consent, separate from our MSA?

12:56 Megan O'Connor: Yes, separate.

12:58 Michael Grant: Okay.

13:00 Avery Johnson: Next steps from us: we’ll send (1) a redline-ready consent form, (2) a draft story outline with two variants — fully anonymized and, later, potentially named — and (3) proposed metrics language that’s qualitative or range-based. Then we’ll schedule a follow-up.

13:17 Megan O'Connor: Sounds good.

13:19 Dr. Lila Patel: Thank you.

13:20 Jason Wu: Yep, thanks.

13:22 Avery Johnson: Thanks everyone.

[End of transcript]

Notes
- Helios preference: anonymized public case study (no logo/name; no employee names; generic titles only)
- Metrics: ranges only; avoid absolute values; no cost numbers; no volumes; include measurement caveat
- Claims: avoid “HIPAA compliant,” avoid mentioning BAA publicly; permissible to describe controls (audit logs, KMS integration) without cloud/provider specifics
- Approvals: 10 business day review window; explicit written approval required; revocation clause required
